newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. city council bashes Switzerland in hot debate.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. city council bashes Switzerland in hot debate.

text.p: One New York City Councilman demanded the Swiss "do the right thing and come clean," another accused the Swiss of keeping Jews out during the Second World War while holding on to their money and a tearful Holocaust survivor told how the Swiss mistreated her only last week.

Swiss bashing dominated a meeting of the New York City Council on Monday as it debated a bill on whether to keep city funds out of Swiss banks. But the council ended the day without taking any action, although committee chairwoman Mary Pinkett insisted the measure would eventually come to a vote.

"Harsh but fair," said Swiss Consul General Alfred Defago diplomatically of the three-hour debate in which some council members attacked his country, while others grilled him on why a Swiss bank guard was held by police and questioned when he reported an illegal shredding of wartime bank documents.

"Switzerland was not a saviour. You didn't let Jewish people in and you took their money as well," said Brooklyn Democrat Noach Dear, an Orthodox Jew who said the mayor of New York should give the bank guard a medal.

Reminding Defago that the council was comprised of people of all races and religions, Dear said, "Maybe you should open your eyes, there are not just Jews trying to blackmail you." He was referring to a widely quoted remark by a former Swiss president accusing Jewish groups of "blackmail and extortion" for demanding a Holocaust memorial fund.
He was followed by Manhattan Councilwoman Kathryn Freed who criticised the Swedish government before quickly correcting herself and saying, "er ... the Swiss government."

Dear then interrupted, asking the diplomats whether their country's banks "felt an honest obligation" to set up the fund or "were they just bowing to pressure." Bronx Councilman Israel Ruiz Jr. told them that despite his first name, he was Hispanic and then added that the Swiss should "do the right thing and come clean."

New York Republican Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, a stern critic of the Swiss, appeared as a witness before the committee, telling it that the $71 million Swiss compensation fund was not sufficent and adding, "We have a sacred duty to see to it that there is a total fair accounting."
But he and World Jewish Congress (WJC) representatives told the council this was not the right moment for sanctions.

WJC Secretary General Israel Singer revealed that former U.S. State Department Bosnia peace negotiator Richard Holbrooke played a previously unknown role in helping to find a solution to the impasse between Jewish groups and Swiss banks that was broken last week with the fund announcement.
Singer did not expand on Holbrooke's role. Holbrooke is an investment banker with a U.S. subsidiary of Credit Suisse.

Estelle Sapir, a 79-year-old Holocaust survivor, told the council she had been trying to retrieve her father's money from Credit Suisse since 1946 but has been stonewalled because she could not produce a death certificate. Her father died in a German death camp.
Last week, she said Swiss airport immigration officials detained her for two hours while trying to decide whether to let her into the country. They finally relented and gave her a four-day visa.

A Credit Suisse official at the hearing vowed to personally do all he could to get the case resolved, saying the problem was that an account in her father's name was closed many years ago and records were missing.
"I felt like I was being questioned again by the Germans," she said of her detention at the airport.
